I’ve smoked a rack of ribs on one and the smoke doesn’t touch the food unless it actually wants to.

For rentals, a decent 22-inch charcoal kettle costs maybe fifteen bucks a day, and it’s plenty for twenty-five people if you burn it hot and stagger the cooking. Bring a charcoal chimney starter; a cheap one lasts forever and saves you from dumping lighter fluid all over a nice meal.

You’ll want a kitchen thermometer—digital probe, not the cheap spring-loaded ones. Meat’s done when it’s the right temp, not when it looks like it. Chicken breast to 165°F, pork shoulder to 195°F for pulling, burgers to 160°F. Stick it in the thickest part, wait ten seconds, done.

Tongs are next; grab a pair with silicone tips so they don’t scratch the grate. A spatula’s handy for flipping burgers without piercing them. And a decent pair of heat-resistant gloves—if you’ve got a cast-iron grate that’s been roaring, you don’t want to yank it barehanded.

For holding food, a couple of insulated food carriers or stockpots with lids are lifesavers. You can move burgers straight from the grill to the carrier, keep them hot, and nobody’s eating cold meat. I use a 22-quart roaster when I’m feeding a crowd; fits a whole rack of ribs and a dozen burgers with room for buns.

Don’t forget a good scraper and a wire brush for the grate; grill residue builds up fast and it’s a pain to clean later. A quick scrape between batches keeps things sanitary and stops flare-ups.

If you’re going to smoke, you’ll want wood chips or chunks—apple or hickory for a mild, sweet smoke. Soak them twenty minutes, add them to the coals once the grill’s hot, and you’ve got a wood-smoked flavor without the shellfish issue.

Peanut butter is another favourite; a dab on a spoon between sessions works wonders, but watch the sugar and salt content.

Stuff her evening meal inside a Kong or a snuffle mat; the effort to get the kibble out satisfies her need to forage and keeps her busy for twenty minutes. Speaking of foraging, wild crows will cache surplus food in hundreds of different spots and then retrieve it weeks later using landscape cues—your pup could learn from them!

text:
By the way, grain-free kibble is off the table for Benny—my vet friend passed along the same warning about DCM risks in retriever breeds. That’s actually a solid instinct to skip; good move.

Now, what you want front and centre on that ingredient list is a named animal protein—chicken, beef, turkey, or fish—listed first, because that’s his main protein source and growing Labs need plenty of it. Right after that, you’ll often see a vegetable starch like chickpea or pea, which works fine for texture and some fibre without the heart fuss of grain-free.

I’d also keep an eye out for omega-3s and omega-6s listed as fish oil or chicken fat. Those fatty acids help with joint health and coat shine, and Labs put a lot of stress on their hips as they sprint around the yard.

Speaking of hips, imagine a crow—Corvus corax—dropping walnuts onto a road and waiting for cars to crack them open. They time traffic lights, cache food, and remember human faces for years. Not that Benny will need to remember yours, but the idea of smart, adaptable feeding habits feels oddly fitting.

Avoid anything that lists “meat by-products” without specifying the animal, and steer clear of artificial colours or flavour enhancers; they’re just marketing fluff. A clean list with real meat, a starch, a handful of veggies, and an oil source is the sweet spot.

If the label mentions glucosamine or added joint support, that’s a nice bonus for a large-breed puppy, though not essential—most balanced puppy formulas already include enough to cover growth needs.

One more thing: check that the calcium-to-phosphorus ratio sits between 1.1:1 and 1.4:1. Too much calcium and you risk skeletal issues; too little and bones don’t set properly. It’s usually listed in the guaranteed analysis, so flip the bag and look for those numbers.

You’re doing all the right homework here. Just remember, crows can recognise and remember individual human faces for years, so if you’re kind to Benny now, he’ll remember you forever—though probably with more enthusiasm than a crow.
